doc.title: James Hunter interviewed by Monk Rowe, Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: What keeps a song off a record; formula and rhymes
summary: Hunter rejects generic songs, describes his two-straight-verses-and-a-joke formula, and the cul-de-sac rhyme from 'One Way Love'.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Okay so I’ll wrap up here. What makes one of your compositions, one of your tunes, not get on a record?

Oh if it’s a bit too generic. But for shorter stuff I’ll put it in. If it sounds like anyone could have written it, if it really sounds — doesn’t have any distinctive touches or, you know, then I’ll feel like — because sometimes I’ve deliberately tried, just for the sake of writing something, to write something generic like anyone would have written, like a stand upon it, and then you can’t help putting your own stamp on it. By the third verse — I mean I write to a formula. I tend to do this a bit like sitcoms comedy, two straight lines and a funny one. And I’ll do that in verses. I’ll do two straight verses and then I’ll throw a joke in the third one you know. And it often happens with me. So I’ll do that.
You are the only guy I know who rhymed with cul-de-sac.
What song was that? Oh yeah, cul-de-sac/don’t come back wasn’t it.
I finally made it back/from that lonely cul-de-sac.
Oh no that’s “One Way Love.” Somebody must’ve done it. But I’m the only person I know who did it.
